cards.when: comparing the forecast accuracy of TWO methods (DM) or an honest out-of-sample backtest of one model per horizon (tsCV)
cards.when_not: more than two models together (→ #75); assumption diagnostics for a single model (→ #76/#77); an in-sample or nested comparison

alternatives.criterion: when you compare >2 models (it avoids the multiple-testing bias of the pairwise DM)
loss-based ranking without a statistical significance test

output_key_fields: statistic: the DM stat (~t); the sign/direction depends on the order of e1,e2
p_value: < a rejects equal accuracy
parameter: (horizon, power)
errors: a series (h=1) or frame (h>1) of forecast errors with leading blanks
accuracy: data_frame per-horizon rmse/mae/me/n_eff over the finite values
interpretation_traps: alternative=less => method 2 is less accurate than 1 (e1 is better); greater => the reverse; the sign depends on the order of e1,e2
me != 0 => a bias in the forecast
n_eff falls at large h => a less reliable RMSE
DM is not for in-sample/nested comparison (Diebold 2015)

cards.when: many (>=2) models together -> the subset statistically indistinguishable from the best at (1-alpha), via a block bootstrap of the loss matrix
cards.when_not: exactly 2 models (→ dm_test, simpler, no bootstrap); it does not say which one is 'the best'

alternatives.criterion: for exactly 2 models, a pairwise test
many models against ONE benchmark (not covered here)

output_key_fields: show: data_frame of the surviving models only (model, Avg.Loss, ranks, MCS p-Value)
included: the names of the models in the final confidence set
statistic: Tmax or TR; ssm: the raw model handle (a stub once serialised)
interpretation_traps: show contains ONLY the surviving models, not the eliminated ones
the MCS p-Value is NOT the p-value of an individual model; a model is in the set if its MCS p-Value > alpha
a different seed/B => a slightly different set (bootstrap variability) - supply a seed
Tmax vs TR can give different sets
LossLevel/LossVol are non-conformable for a multi-column evaluated argument => the wrapper calls them per column + cbind
sources: Bernardi & Catania 2014 (the model confidence set procedure)

cards.when: residual diagnostics for a regression (lm/glm): serial correlation (BG), heteroskedasticity (BP), wrong functional form (RESET)
cards.when_not: ARCH in a time series (→ #77); unit root or stationarity (→ category 01); models beyond least squares/GLM (→ the VAR serial-correlation test, #11)

alternatives.criterion: more general heteroskedasticity (approximated by BP + varformula)
autocorrelation in a plain residual series without a regression design matrix
when the heteroskedasticity is time-dependent (volatility clustering)

output_key_fields: statistic: BG LM=n*R2 (Chisq)/F; BP Chisq; RESET F
p_value: < a rejects H0 => a problem EXISTS
parameter: df; method/data_name; plus the raw test record
interpretation_traps: polarity: rejection = BAD (the model fails the diagnostic); H0='all is well'
BG with a very small order misses high-order autocorrelation
Breusch-Pagan with studentize=False is sensitive to non-normality — prefer True
a RESET rejection => misspecification BUT not of what kind
a serial-correlation rejection => the OLS standard errors are invalid (use HAC/Newey-West), not necessarily biased coefficients
sources: Enders 2015 (BG > DW with a lagged y)

cards.when: testing for ARCH effects (conditional heteroskedasticity / volatility clustering) in a univariate series/residuals; a pre-check before GARCH
cards.when_not: cross-sectional heteroskedasticity (→ bptest); autocorrelation in the level (→ bgtest/Ljung-Box); multivariate volatility

alternatives.criterion: equivalent evidence of ARCH; ARCH-LM is preferred as a formal LM test with clear df
after a positive ARCH-LM -> fit a volatility model

output_key_fields: statistic: Chi-squared LM=n*R2 of the auxiliary regression
parameter: df = lags
p_value: < a rejects H0 => ARCH effects EXIST (you want GARCH)
lags/demean echoes; plus the raw test record
interpretation_traps: polarity: rejection = an ARCH effect is present (H0='no ARCH'); a small p => conditional heteroskedasticity
run it on residuals, not the raw series - ARCH in the raw series may be due to an unmodelled mean
large lags => lower power
sources: Tsay, Analysis of Financial Time Series (ARCH-LM pre-GARCH)

cards.method: Density-forecast evaluation — CRPS / LogS / PIT (sample + parametric + tail-weighted)
cards.when: evaluating a predictive DISTRIBUTION (posterior/ensemble draws or parametric) as a whole distribution; proper scoring (CRPS/LogS) + PIT calibration + tail-weighted CRPS for GaR downside risk
cards.when_not: a point-forecast comparison -> #74 Diebold-Mariano; selecting among many point models -> #75 model confidence set; binary AUC -> #84; in-sample fit -> #76/#77; multivariate ES and VS are outside the surface

alternatives.criterion: a robust default for draws; the same units as y
a likelihood-based/local score; BUT sensitive to the KDE bandwidth in the tails
the predictive distribution is explicitly normal/t/mixnorm (an analytic BVAR predictive)
an asymmetric cost in the tail (GaR left-tail focus)
point forecasts only (comparing 2 models)
GaR quantiles -> a full density; then parametric scoring here

output_key_fields: scores: per-observation score vector (chart-data, score per time period)
mean_score: the mean score (the comparative number; LOWER=BETTER)
score: 'CRPS'/'LogS'/'twCRPS'; method (edf/kde) or family (normal/t/mixnorm)
weighted/side/a/b/kind: tail-weighted metadata (twcrps threshold / owcrps outcome)
pit (sr_pit_sample): the PIT values in [0,1]; a histogram close to uniform => good calibration
n / n_draws: number of observations / draws
interpretation_traps: ORIENTATION: CRPS & LogS are NEGATIVELY oriented — LOWER = BETTER (not accuracy)
LogS = -Inf if y falls outside the support of the draws; KDE smooths that but is sensitive to the bandwidth in the tails -> for heavy tails prefer CRPS(edf)
the CRPS of a single observation is in the same units as y -> it is NOT comparable across series of different scale
PIT: a ∪ shape => underdispersed (too tight a distribution); a ∩ shape => overdispersed; uniform => calibrated
a low tail-weighted score may simply reflect few observations in the tail — read the per-obs scores
bw: crps/logs_sample requires a bw vector[1:n]; the wrapper recycles a scalar -> length(y)
sources: Jordan, Krüger & Lerch 2019 JSS 90(12) (evaluating probabilistic forecasts with proper scoring rules)
Gneiting & Raftery 2007 JASA 102:359-378 (proper scoring rules, CRPS/LogS)
Krüger, Lerch, Thorarinsdottir & Gneiting 2021 Int. J. Forecast. (predictive-distribution scoring)
Diebold, Gunther & Tay 1998 Int. Econ. Rev. 39(4):863-883 (PIT calibration evaluation — the basis of sr_pit_sample, custom implementation)
precondition_tools: c03_multivariate_nowcasting/bayesian_var.bvar_predict (or #13/#14/#17/#60: they produce the posterior predictive draws the scores are evaluated on)
c12_distribution_risk/quantile_regression.qr_growth_at_risk (GaR quantiles; the density comes via #95 -> parametric scoring)

cards.method: Point-accuracy metric table across horizons and series
cards.when: the baseline of every forecast evaluation, and the input to every test of predictive ability
cards.when_not: the forecasts are densities rather than points (-> scoring rules); the series have no common scale and unscaled metrics would be meaningless

alternatives.criterion: one series, natural units
several series with different scales
the scale is ratio and there are no zeros

output_key_fields: metrics: the table by horizon, series and method
mase, rmsse: scaled metrics, comparable across series
theil_u: against a naive benchmark
bias: mean error, which the squared metrics hide
interpretation_traps: MAPE IS UNDEFINED AT ZERO AND ASYMMETRIC -- it penalises over-forecasts more than under-forecasts, which systematically favours forecasts biased low
averaging a scale-dependent metric across series lets the largest series dominate; that is what the scaled metrics exist to prevent
the mean error is the only metric that reveals bias, and reporting only squared or absolute metrics hides it entirely
sources: Makridakis, Spiliotis & Assimakopoulos 2020 (International Journal of Forecasting 36:54)

cards.method: Proper scoring rules: CRPS, log score, pinball and tail-weighted CRPS
cards.when: evaluating a density or quantile forecast, where a point metric throws away everything the forecast said about uncertainty
cards.when_not: the forecast is a point with no distribution; the evaluation sample is too small for score differences to be distinguishable

alternatives.criterion: the default for a full predictive distribution
strictly proper and local, but unbounded
the forecast is a set of quantiles

output_key_fields: scores: per observation and averaged
decomposition: reliability and resolution components where available
tail_weighted: scores emphasising a region of interest
skill: score against a reference forecast
interpretation_traps: THE LOG SCORE IS UNBOUNDED: a single observation in a region the forecast gave near-zero density produces an infinite score and destroys the average -- CRPS is bounded and usually preferred for that reason
a proper scoring rule cannot be gamed by hedging, but an improper one can -- and several popular ad hoc measures are improper
tail-weighted scores answer a different question from the unweighted version and rank forecasts differently
sources: Gneiting & Ranjan 2011 (Journal of Business and Economic Statistics 29:411)

cards.method: Clark-West and Giacomini-White conditional predictive ability
cards.when: comparing NESTED forecasting models, where Diebold-Mariano is invalid because the difference in expected loss is zero under the null
cards.when_not: the models are non-nested, where Diebold-Mariano applies directly

alternatives.criterion: non-nested models
nested models, adjusted for the estimation noise
conditional predictive ability, finite-sample based

output_key_fields: statistic, p_value: the predictive-ability test
adjustment: the Clark-West correction term
conditional: whether ability varies with a state variable
loss_differential: the underlying series
interpretation_traps: DIEBOLD-MARIANO IS INVALID FOR NESTED MODELS -- the standard normal critical values are wrong and the test is badly undersized, which is exactly the case of adding one indicator to an autoregression
Clark-West tests equal predictive ability of the POPULATION models, not the estimated ones, which is a different and often less interesting null
Giacomini-White conditions on a state and can find ability that averages to zero unconditionally

cards.method: Superior predictive ability, reality check and StepM
cards.when: many forecasts are compared against a benchmark at once, and the best of many will beat it by chance alone
cards.when_not: there are two models, where a pairwise test suffices

alternatives.criterion: the original, conservative under poor models
less sensitive to poor models in the set
you want to identify WHICH models beat the benchmark

output_key_fields: statistic, p_value: the joint test against the benchmark
superior_models: those surviving the stepwise procedure
n_models: how many were compared -- the source of the multiplicity
bootstrap: the resampling scheme used
interpretation_traps: THE BEST OF FIFTY MODELS WILL BEAT A BENCHMARK BY CHANCE; that is precisely the data-snooping bias these tests correct, and reporting the best model's individual p-value is the error
the Reality Check is sensitive to including many poor models, which drag the null distribution -- SPA was designed to fix that
these tests need a stationary or block bootstrap because the loss differentials are serially dependent
sources: Hansen 2005 (Journal of Business and Economic Statistics 23:365)

cards.when: testing whether a forecast is unbiased and efficient, and whether one forecast contains everything another has to offer
cards.when_not: the forecast sample is too short for the regressions to have power; the forecasts are not for the same target

alternatives.criterion: unbiasedness and efficiency of one forecast
whether one forecast subsumes another
efficiency with respect to specific information

output_key_fields: mz_test: joint test that the intercept is zero and the slope one
bias: the estimated intercept
encompassing: whether one forecast's weight in a combination is one
efficiency: orthogonality against the tested information set
interpretation_traps: THE MINCER-ZARNOWITZ REGRESSION NEEDS HAC STANDARD ERRORS at horizons beyond one, because overlapping forecasts induce a moving-average error by construction
rejecting rationality can mean the loss function is asymmetric rather than the forecast irrational -- the test assumes squared loss
encompassing tests with highly correlated forecasts are uninformative because the combination weights are barely identified
sources: Mincer & Zarnowitz 1969, The evaluation of economic forecasts (Economic Forecasts and Expectations)

cards.method: Interval and quantile evaluation: coverage, Winkler and weighted interval score
cards.when: the forecast is an interval or a set of quantiles, and coverage alone can be bought by making the interval wide
cards.when_not: the forecast is a full density (-> scoring rules); the evaluation sample is too short for coverage to be estimated

alternatives.criterion: a first check, necessary but not sufficient
coverage and width in one number
several intervals summarised together

output_key_fields: coverage: realised against nominal, per level
winkler: interval score per observation
wis: the weighted interval score and its decomposition
width: mean interval width
interpretation_traps: COVERAGE AND WIDTH MUST BE READ TOGETHER: an interval from minus to plus infinity covers perfectly and is useless, which is why the Winkler score penalises width
the weighted interval score decomposes into spread, over-prediction and under-prediction, and that decomposition is where the diagnosis is
coverage estimated on a short sample has enormous sampling error; 19 of 20 is not evidence of 95% coverage
sources: Bracher, Ray, Gneiting & Reich 2021 (PLOS Computational Biology 17:e1008618)

cards.method: Density comparison and calibration: Amisano-Giacomini and Berkowitz
cards.when: comparing density forecasts formally, and testing whether a predictive distribution is calibrated
cards.when_not: the forecasts are points; the sample is too short for the PIT distribution to be assessed

alternatives.criterion: comparing two density forecasts
calibration of one density, with a power advantage over raw PIT tests
a visual calibration check

output_key_fields: log_score_difference: with its test statistic
berkowitz: the calibration test
pit: probability-integral-transform values
autocorrelation: dependence in the PIT series, which independence requires
interpretation_traps: A UNIFORM PIT HISTOGRAM IS NECESSARY BUT NOT SUFFICIENT: the PIT series must also be independent, and a calibrated-looking histogram with autocorrelated PITs is a failed forecast
the Berkowitz test transforms PITs to normality and gains power over a raw uniformity test, which is why it is preferred
weighted log-score comparisons emphasising a region are not proper unless constructed carefully
sources: Amisano & Giacomini 2007 (Journal of Business and Economic Statistics 25:177-190)
Berkowitz 2001 (Journal of Business and Economic Statistics 19:465)

cards.when: the standard checks a fitted regression must pass before its coefficients are reported
cards.when_not: the model is not a regression; the diagnostics are already run by the estimator

alternatives.criterion: White, Breusch-Pagan, Goldfeld-Quandt
RESET, Harvey-Collier, linktest
you would rather correct than test

output_key_fields: heteroskedasticity: test statistics and p-values
functional_form: RESET and related tests
normality: residual normality tests
influence: leverage, Cook's distance and DFBETAS
interpretation_traps: HETEROSKEDASTICITY DOES NOT BIAS THE COEFFICIENTS, only the standard errors; a rejected test calls for robust errors, not for a different estimator
White's test has power against functional-form misspecification as well as heteroskedasticity, so a rejection does not identify the cause
with a large sample every diagnostic rejects; read the magnitude of the problem, not only the p-value

cards.method: Non-nested model tests: Cox, Davidson-MacKinnon J and Vuong
cards.when: two models neither of which nests the other, where an information criterion gives a ranking but no test
cards.when_not: the models are nested (-> a likelihood-ratio or Clark-West test); they have different dependent variables

alternatives.criterion: regression models, simple to run
the classical non-nested likelihood test
likelihood models, including a test that they are equivalent

output_key_fields: statistic, p_value: per direction of the test
conclusion: which model, if either, is rejected
vuong: the likelihood-ratio-based statistic with its variance correction
both_rejected: whether neither model survives
interpretation_traps: THESE TESTS CAN REJECT BOTH MODELS OR NEITHER, and both outcomes are informative -- a test that rejects model A against B is not evidence that B is correct
the J test is a regression-based approximation and has poor size in small samples
Vuong's test requires the models to be non-nested in a strict sense; applied to nested models its distribution is wrong
sources: Cox 1961 (Proceedings of the Fourth Berkeley Symposium 1:105)

cards.method: Meta-analysis and publication bias: meta-regression, PET-PEESE, Egger and funnel
cards.when: synthesising many estimates of the same parameter, and testing whether the literature is distorted by selective reporting
cards.when_not: the estimates are of different parameters and cannot be pooled; there are too few studies for bias tests to have power

alternatives.criterion: the studies estimate one common parameter
the true effect varies across studies
you suspect publication bias

output_key_fields: pooled: the synthesised estimate with its interval
heterogeneity: tau squared and I squared
egger: the small-study-effects test
pet_peese: bias-corrected estimate
interpretation_traps: A SIGNIFICANT EGGER TEST IS NOT PROOF OF PUBLICATION BIAS -- small-study effects also arise when smaller studies genuinely differ in design or population
PET-PEESE is known to over-correct when there is no bias and under-correct with strong heterogeneity; it is a diagnostic, not a definitive correction
fixed and random effects answer different questions, and with high heterogeneity the fixed-effect interval is far too narrow
sources: Borenstein, Hedges, Higgins & Rothstein 2009, Introduction to Meta-Analysis

arguments.name: forecastfunction
arguments.description: The model/pipeline that is backtested: rolling-origin cross-validation of ONE forecasting function with signature function(y, h) that returns a forecast object (card 74). Given ONLY as a name from a closed allowlist, never as executable code. Options: naive = Naive / random walk: f(t+k)=y(T). The classic benchmark (FPP3). · seasonal-naive = Seasonal naive: f(t+k)=y(T+k-m). Benchmark for seasonal series; at frequency=1 it degenerates IDENTICALLY to naive (lag=1). · drift = Random walk with drift: naive + mean historical change (FPP3 benchmark). · mean = Mean forecast: f(t+k)=mean(y). Benchmark; bootstrap=True (5000 stochastic paths) is PINNED to False for determinism. · ses = Simple exponential smoothing = ETS(A,N,N) (without trend/seasonality). · holt = Holt linear trend = ETS(A,A,N) (linear trend, without seasonality). · ets = Automatic ETS state-space (error/trend/season selection with AICc); same method as the run_ets node (cat. 02). · auto_arima = Automatic (S)ARIMA with stepwise Hyndman-Khandakar; same method as the run_auto_arima node (cat. 02). · theta = Theta method (Assimakopoulos & Nikolopoulos 2000, M3 winner); same family as the run_theta node (cat. 02). Caution: tsCV re-fits at EVERY origin -> ets/auto_arima are significantly slower than the benchmarks.
